analysis.one_liner: Phases out the separate subminimum wage for tipped workers to the full federal minimum wage.
analysis.headline: A bill to phase out the $2.13 federal tipped minimum wage never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, employers may pay workers who earn tips as little as $2.13 an hour in cash, counting customer tips toward the rest of the minimum wage. This bill would end that arrangement. It would start tipped cash wages at $3.60 an hour and raise them $1.50 each year until they reach the full federal minimum wage, and it would tighten rules so employers and managers cannot keep any portion of workers' tips. It was sent to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who earn tips — servers, bartenders, bussers, delivery drivers, casino dealers, and salon workers — especially in the roughly half of states that use the federal $2.13 tipped minimum with no higher state standard. Those workers would get a guaranteed cash wage that rises each year until it equals the federal minimum, regardless of how much customers tip.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tipped workers paid as little as $2.13 an hour

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the separate minimum wage for tipped employees, so the cash wage an employer must pay a tipped worker becomes the full federal minimum wage under the Fair Labor Standards Act.
Raises the tipped cash wage during the transition: $3.60 an hour in the first year, then $1.50 more each year until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage.
Bars employers from keeping any tips for any purpose, including allowing managers to keep a share or using workers' tips to cover credit and debit card transaction fees.

Treats a mandatory charge on customers as a tip — payable to employees in full — when the charge could reasonably make a customer believe it goes directly to workers, and requires employers to disclose what portion of such charges reaches staff.

Lets non-supervisory employees petition (30% of them) for a vote on establishing or changing a tip pool, with the pool passing at 51%, and requires the employer to administer it at its own expense without coercion.
Counts an employee as 'tipped' only if no more than 20% of their hours go to non-tipped work, limiting how much time workers can spend on ungratified duties at the lower wage.

analysis.who_pays: Employers of tipped workers, chiefly full-service restaurants, bars, and delivery and salon businesses, which would owe a steadily rising cash wage. Some of that cost would likely reach customers through menu prices; the bill also shifts card-processing fees on tipped transactions from workers to employers.

drawbacks.text: The transition is slow by design: the cash wage starts at $3.60 and climbs only $1.50 a year, so a worker could spend several years still earning below the full minimum.

Eliminating the tip credit raises labor costs for tipped-worker employers, hitting small independent restaurants hardest and likely pushing some cost onto customers through higher prices (a standard effect of a higher wage floor).

The bill's tip-pool process puts the employer in charge of administering pools and even lets the employer impose a resolution in disputes among participating employees after two rounds of internal negotiation fail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core effect is straightforward: millions of tipped workers in states without a higher state standard would gain a guaranteed cash wage that grows yearly instead of a $2.13 floor that has not risen since 1991. The cost falls on their employers, especially small restaurants, and partly on diners. The slow phase-in and the employer's role in administering tip pools are real design compromises, but they do not change the direction of the bill: it transfers money from employers to low-wage workers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees on the day it was introduced, and neither one ever scheduled action, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jahana Hayes introduced the Tipped Worker Protection Act on September 8, 2023, with nine Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee for consideration.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote occurred, and the action history shows no activity after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Restaurant and other tipped-worker employers are better off: the federal tip credit stays in place, and their obligation to tipped cash wages remains $2.13 an hour. Tipped workers are no better off than before.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, and with no vote ever scheduled, no Republican support for the bill appears in the record.

industries.industry: Full-service restaurants and other tipped-worker employers
industries.note: The bill would eliminate the tip credit that lets these employers pay a $2.13 cash wage and count tips toward the minimum, raising their guaranteed labor costs year by year. Employers' interest in keeping the tip credit runs directly against tipped workers' wages.

The bill still lets merchants be charged card processing fees; it only stops employers from covering those fees out of workers' tips, shifting the cost to employers. Card fee revenue itself is untouched.
